At the time, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna there were units called HOS that were operating as well. I've already pointed out that as for the members of the national defence of Citluk I could not win them over so as to have them fight under the name of national defence [as interpreted]. I've already presented the reasons for this. So I'm aware of the specific document and have been so since the 11th or 12th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We're not talking about the national defence, as was noted on line -- I believe it's 19, but I believe we're talking about the Territorial Defence and that's what you were referring to during the first session; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And basically the comments that you gave us earlier concerning how the Territorial Defence had been discredited, we can see that in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: This document also refers to some examples as to how the Territorial Defence that existed up until then had compromised itself. Also, it says that this name could not motivate people to fight under that name. As we can see in this order, what was ordered was a single designation and a single name for all the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I think that helps us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Concerning this document which we are now talking about that is P 005 -- P 00155, and in that one, the second paragraph of that "Command" starts with the following sentence, and I quote: "The Decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the BH Territorial Defence, also of 8 April 1992, is a rash one," a rash one, r-a-s-h, "in political terms at this moment. Since the beginning of the attack on the Croatian people that same Presidency has been silent in respect of crimes against the Croats." Now, my question would be directed to the witness, if he would be able to remind us about that decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course I know that he may not have the text before him now, but since it was, I believe, the major -- one of the major motives and arguments why the command of the HVO was come to life and established, that is why I believe that it would be worthwhile to recall what kind of decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina represented a kind of rash decision, why was it considered as a needless and useless document to rely upon it? So it is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Presidency itself gave the best answer to this question. Soon after this date they changed the name of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say that soon after this the Presidency itself gave up on the name Territorial Defence and started calling its armed forces the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is my opinion that this happened for the reasons that I already mentioned, namely, that this name had been compromised due to the activities of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Well, although I would like to see the text itself, but since it is not being possible then I thank you for your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is in the e-court, that document, and we did discuss it extensively with -- I believe when Mr. Akmadzic was here. So it is 1D 01219, so if Your Honour wishes to look at it and then further question Mr. Buntic, we could pull it up and make it available to everybody. I don't have it physically with me, but it's 1D 01219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go on to the next document, and that is 1D 00899, 1D 00899. This is a document dated 15 May 1992, it's a statutory decision. If you could look at it. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You do have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I have it in front of me, that is to say -- well, has the question already been put or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. First, do you have it? I like to do things step by step. So -- okay, now that you have it, can you please explain to us what this document is. What is this statutory decision dated May 15, 1992? And of course, in providing the answer to that, perhaps you can explain to us in the preamble where it talks about 18 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: As for this document, I've already said that this is one of the documents that were handed over to me when I in fact took over my duties of head of the department for justice and general administration of the HZ HB. I'm aware of this document, it is a statutory decision, and it has to do - and I underline this - the provisional establishment of executive government and administration in the territory of HZ HB. In Article 1 what is defined are the powers and duties of the Croatian Defence Council, and it says that the HVO shall be in charge of carrying out executive duties in the territory of HZ HB. Article 2 states that members of the Croatian Defence Council shall be elected by the Presidency of the HZ HB at the proposal of the president of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me stop you here so we go to Article 3, and again I want to go step by step. It says here that: "The Croatian Defence Council shall report to the Presidency ..." What did you understand that to mean? Was that -- because later on we see that it is -- that it has collective -- they're collectively responsible for decisions adopted. So can you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Article 3, in my opinion, prescribes what was envisaged in classical terms, that the executive is always responsible to the legislation that elected them. It is correct that in paragraph 2 it says that members of the Croatian Defence Council, or rather, the president, vice-presidents, heads of departments, and other members of the Croatian Defence Council are jointly responsible for the decisions passed by the Croatian Defence Council and that in particular they are responsible for their area of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here. Well, how do we interpret this? Because where I come from you don't have a collective executive body. There usually is somebody who is at the top. So first of all, when it says here president, vice-president, heads of department, and other members shall collectively be responsible for decisions, what does that mean? If a decision has to be made, how is a decision made by this collective body? Who votes? And then whose decision is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: In this specific case as far as the HVO of the HZ HB is concerned, decisions were passed by majority vote of all the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, would that also include -- let me stop you. Would that include department heads and other members, so they would all vote?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: All heads of departments had the right to vote at sessions and also the heads of the subdepartments. Again, I'm going back to the following: Decisions were made by majority vote and decisions were signed by the president of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me stop you here. Whose decision was it? Because you said it was signed by the president and we need to clarify this point because of certain testimony and certain positions taken by the Office of the Prosecution. So whose decision was it now that we know that it was the president who signed the decision after it was collectively voted upon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: In this case these were decisions of the HVO as a collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to the next document, 1D 00174, very quickly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, for the interruption. Mr. President, just for the record I noticed with the last exhibit 1D 00899, which I think according to the Defence list is not in evidence, but in -- the same document is in evidence as P 00206 and that version's accompanied by an official translation as well as opposed to the unofficial translation with this one. And so just for the record it may be of use to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, whether it's official or unofficial, we're willing to have both of them re-examined, Your Honour. There's an obvious reason why we insist on certain matters being translated -- certain documents being retranslated in order to recalibrate the translation, but I take the gentleman's point. We appreciate his observation. We take to heart what he has in mind and we would ask that in such instances that both translations be -- undergo further scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before we're leaving the previous documents, I would like to ask the witness. Who are or who were the other members? It is a very unspecific term. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article, Article number 3, only lists the offices involved. As for the departments, I mentioned which ones existed, but I'm prepared to repeat that. In the Croatian Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think it was Article 2 where you also have the reference to other members, and we have come on it before, and they are other, I think, than the heads of department. It is heads of departments and other. So I'm only interested in the others. Who are the other members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is meant here are the heads of subdepartments because we've already said that departments of economic and social affairs had several subdepartments. Right now I cannot recall each and every one of them, but I do know that there were several of them. Furthermore, the HVO had its commissions as well as certain offices that it established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many they were all in all? How many people constituted the HVO in the sense of Article 2, paragraph 1, of this statutory decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I wasn't sure how many subdepartments there were, so I would have to speculate to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you give an approximate answer? Were they 20? 30? 15? 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in the department of the economy - and I'm speculating now - there were three, four, or five subdepartments and the same number in the social affairs, maybe three subdepartments of that department. I know there were subdepartments of health, of education, of social welfare, and so on. But if I had to give you a precise number and the precise names of these subdepartments, I'm afraid I would be wrong. We will see that from a document adopted at a session of the Presidency in August, the 14th of August. I think that document lists the departments and subdepartments and their competencies, so probably there is a document on the basis of which this can be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Judge Trechsel, we will provide a concrete and accurate answer to that question perhaps through the next witness as well. We do take note of the importance of that question. Unfortunately, I must confess that did escape me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Anyway, 1D 00174, just very quickly. Here we see that this is a decision of your appointment and the date is 15 May 1992, and I take it this is a correct document, you stand by it; correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's the document. It was also handed over to me when I took up my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, P 00250, P 00250, this is a statutory decision on municipal executive authority and municipal administration. And we see that this is dated 13 June 1992, and it might be interesting for the Trial Chamber to some extent. Without going through the document in detail, I wish to point out specifically Article 6 where it says: "The HZ HB HVO shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO work." And it then goes on to say: "... shall instruct the municipal HVO in the field of its competence." If you can tell us, what was the intention of Article 6, if you know, and more importantly, realistically how was this -- how could one -- how could the HZ HB HVO implement Article 6, given the realities of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think that first of all one should go back to the situation that existed before the 15th or 13th of June, 1992. We have to go back to the time from the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the time when conflicts broke out all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, both defence and civilian life had to function. At a time of total isolation when all the central organs of government were cut off, the Assembly, the government, and the Presidency, someone had to take over the organization of civilian life in that area and someone had to defend the country. In particular cases this was done by the municipalities. Each municipality adopted its own regulations. I can't say what number of such regulations were adopted by the municipalities, but it's a fact that in that time, in that period of time, the municipalities had to regulate all military and civilian matters and that a vast number of regulations were adopted in each municipality. The municipality simply had to deal with the newly emerging situation, the situation that had just come into being. Let me give you an example. As the commander of the defence of Citluk, people frequently asked me to whom they should pay their taxes. They were unable to pay their federal taxes because the public accountancy service was not functioning in relation to Yugoslavia, and as of April, it ceased to function within Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's just one example. The municipalities had to adopt regulations in the areas of finance, health, education, and so on. Payments were not functioning, traffic communications were not functioning, railroads, and so on. So the municipalities simply had to adopt a large number of regulations to deal with the situation. The purpose of this article was to achieve something close to unity, or at least to attempt to harmonize this vast number of regulations adopted in the meantime. To what extent this could really be done is another question. It was a long-term process that the Croatian Defence Council had to deal with throughout the period from its founding until it ceased to exist. It was not easy to regulate all these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to ask one or two questions because I believe this decision is a very important one. If we take Article 2, then of course it says that: "The municipal HVO shall consist of its president, heads of office, and other members who shall be appointed and dismissed by the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And also Article 7 which says that: "Administrative affairs that fall within the rights and duties of the municipality shall be conducted by administrative offices." And again: "The administrative offices shall be established by decision of the municipal HVO, with the exception of the Defence Office and the Interior." Now, my question is the following: As you know, until that very date, which is date 15 May 1992, I'm sure that there had been municipal executive authorities and administrations throughout the territory, and here you do not find anything which would say what would happen to those who had been dismissed. And therefore, I would like to ask you to give us some advice on that matter because, of course, the -- if somebody was dismissed, either from the municipal council or from the administration, no doubt that it entailed an important issue of leaving, of, I don't know, some payment, et cetera. So it is my question how this statutory decision was implemented in that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first, to the best of my memory there was Article 2. Just as the structure of the HVO was organized at the HZ HB level, the municipal HVOs were organized in a similar way, they consisted of the president, the heads, unlike the HVO of the HZ HB where there were departments, in this decision they are called offices or bureaus. And there are similar definitions. I think that this part is clear. As regards the second question, why not the heads of the bureaus of defence and of interior affairs, this is inherited from the previous system; because in the former system of the former Yugoslavia in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the offices of defence and of the interior of the municipality, they did not have the authority to appoint their heads but according to the previous system and previous regulations this was done by the republican organs. So these departments under the previous system were not within the competence of the municipality. In my opinion, this is simply taken over, copied, by analogy from the previous system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. As a matter of fact, frankly, the thrust of my second question was not about the -- these two exceptions, that is defence and office of the interior, because I -- finally I read this structure as it has been also before. But my major question was about the fate of those who could have been, should have been, may have been dismissed and -- because we -- let us not close our eyes over the fact that it was the situation of a rather confrontational time and I'm sure that many of the people working with the administration they were not all Croats, they were Muslims, they were Serbs, if they remained there at all. And it is my question: Was there any legal remedy for some of the people who had been dismissed there at that time, what happened to them? It is very -- really, it is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If someone considered that their rights had been violated, they had several options. One was to appeal against a decision or document, to institute an administrative procedure, to appeal against it if this had to do with state organs. If they were dismissed from a job in a company, in an enterprise, they could institute a proceedings before a court of associated labour or before a general court. So they could enter into labour litigation. If they were dismissed as a result of a crime or if they felt that their dismissal was the result of a crime, they could file a criminal report against the person responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps at this point in time, given the questioning that is coming on this particular document, it might be good to describe to us a little bit about the municipalities and their relationship with the HVO, the executive authority, and, of course, the role they played within the Presidency. So starting off with the municipalities, how dependent or independent were the municipalities at that point in time? And we're asking for very concrete answers because we have to move along rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the 13th of July -- June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 1992, the time when this decision was adopted. At that point in time there were literally no other structures of government or authority, apart from those functioning within the municipalities, either at the federal level or at the republican level. At that point in time the institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had not been established either. There was no one who could carry out executive business. Only the municipalities were functioning on the 13th of June, 1992, because at that time we didn't have the civilian HVO, it wasn't complete. This would only occur on the 14th or the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier on I asked you about the Presidency. From the municipality level, who was sitting on the Presidency, that is, the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the HZ HB by virtue of its position, or rather, ex officio it included the top persons in the municipal government or the HVO. So the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna consisted of the highest-ranking official in the municipality or the president of the municipal HVO; that is, the highest administrative body in the -- consisted of the representatives of the municipalities which were part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So in this -- so to be very concrete we're talking about the president of the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: The president or the chief, depending on the name used in that particular municipality, the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you also indicated that this collective body, this Presidency that was made up of the presidents, including others that is, but made up of the presidents of the municipalities or the chief persons in the municipalities sat above the HVO, this executive organ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. At any point the Presidency could dismiss any individual member of the HVO as well as the HVO as a whole if it was not satisfied with its work. Had it been dissatisfied with the work of the entire HVO, it would have dismissed them all but any point it would also dismiss any single member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which brings me back to Article 6 and tell us whether you see some sort of a collision. Because it says here: "The HZ HB HVO shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO work" and "... instruct the municipal HVOs in the field of its competence." How can you supervise the legality of a body that sits above you especially when they have the power to dismiss you, as you've just indicated? Do you see that conundrum or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That's clear to me. It's very hard for someone appointing and dismissing you, someone who at any point can dismiss you, for you to tell them they have to do something. In practice, both de facto and de jure, it is an illogical situation; that's true. But that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It was difficult, in my opinion, to expect that the HVO might dismiss the president or mayor of a municipality while at the same time it was responsible for its work to the presidents of the municipalities or the presidents of the municipal HVOs. But that's the situation prescribed by this decision; it's illogical, true, that's what the situation was; it caused numerous problems in practice, but the decision is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for our second break then we'll have an hour left. So we'll have a 20-minute break unless you wanted to ask one question right away, Mr. Karnavas, do you have one last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I don't have any other -- no, Your Honour. I think this is a good time, good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we're going to switch to another topic and this is related to events -- legislation, that came out around 3 July 1992 and we'll start with 1D 01670, 1D 01670.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see that in the English version it says that there was a meeting held on 3 July 1993, that should read 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me. It's correct that this is dated the 3rd of July, 1992, rather than 1993, these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and I take it -- if we go through it we see your name and I take it it would be correct to say that you attended this particular meeting of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we see that on paragraph number 8 there is a discussion from a gentleman by the name of Blago Artukovic from Zenica and then you give a response, I just point that out. I'm not going to ask any questions on this, although the Trial Chamber may have a question or two. I'm more interested in Roman numeral II, that would be on the following page, for us it would be page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hope I'm not too obnoxious, Mr. Karnavas, but it says in this document that there is a list of the attendants which is an integral part of it and which is -- so the document says attached, but I do not have it and I do not think it would be entirely without interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you, and surely you can appreciate the fact that if I had it I really would want to share it with you. However, this is all I have and I apologise. But I'll keep looking for that. But perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- we could ask the gentleman if he recalls, and he might be able to give us some names, if that would be of some assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I -- actually, I don't think so. I would have liked to have seen the total. It might have assisted also with the previous question with other matters, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, going to Roman numeral II: "Decision amending the decision on establishment of HZ HB." And here you are, you're commented -- you're commenting that -- you give the reasons, the objectives, behind the drafting of the decision, that is, of the amendment. Can you explain that a little bit to us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I attended this meeting, or rather, this session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that at this session I took part in the discussion, that I explained to the members of the Presidency the reasons and the purpose of certain regulations adopted at this meeting of the Presidency. I recall that several regulations were adopted and that one of the most important regulations was the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB. On that day at that session this decision was amended. When I say that, I'm referring primarily to Article 7 of the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to get to it step by step. I got to -- let's deal with this document first, and I don't mean to cut you off or to be aggressive, but there is a procedure and we need to keep it rather tight. Now, if we go on to Roman numeral VII, you comment again about the decree on seizure of the occupier's property and its transfer to HZ HB ownership, and again you provide some sort of an explanation. We're going to see those documents, but can you comment a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think I can. I think that items 6 and 7 are very similar, these are two very similar decrees. One is the decree on seizure of the property of the former JNA on the -- and the SSNO on the territory of the HZ HB. With respect to this decree, I consider that the purpose of this decree was primarily to protect the property abandoned by the JNA and taken by the HVO in armed clashes with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think it should be pointed out in this respect that this is socially owned property which cannot be said to be somebody's ownership. The concept of socially owned property is sui generis a concept difficult to explain to anyone who did not participate or work in the legal system of the former Yugoslavia. If we were to simplify this, it was often said to be nobody's property or everybody's property or common property. That's how this term, socially owned property, was translated in everyday speech. It should also be pointed out that all the property which was socially owned rather than owned by the JNA and which consisted in movable items, such as ships, aeroplanes, helicopters, rocket systems, engineering installations, infantry weapons, artillery weapons, that all this was taken by the JNA as if it belonged to them, although it was the property of all the citizens of the former Yugoslavia. This same property was used by the JNA to perpetrate aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina and to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina. These decrees enacted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna meant that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna took this property for its own. It could not take over the property on behalf of a third party, that was not possible, so it took ownership of the property on its own account. And ultimately, this property was subject to the succession of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If I move on now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, but this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- I think not quite unimportant or uninteresting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With regard to the other proposed decrees, the minutes say they were unanimously adopted. Number 7, Roman VII does not have such a mention. Does that mean that it was not adopted or is it a mistake in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all the decrees were passed unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is this -- Judge Trechsel, are you referring to the decree on public companies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the decree on seizure of the occupier's property, but I'm prepared to take the witness's word that they were adopted and must then assume that the minutes are not completely reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could -- if we could go on now to number IX, this is dealing with the decree on organization, work, and purview of the judiciary. We see your name, and if we skim over it we see that you talk about a legal vacuum being created as a result of BH Republic having adopted a decree on the non-application of federal regulations. And then you go on to explain other matters. Now, without going into any great detail, do you stand by what you indicated to us today and what's indicated here in the meeting, in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I stand by that, and I think that the -- this is the decree of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 2nd of May, 1992. In respect of military courts and military prosecutor's offices, there was a legal void which needed to be filled. I believe that it is also important to point out that this decree was never carried out in practice. It was not published in the Official Gazette of the HZ HB, and therefore practically it never came into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It was passed, or rather, what was passed was a new decree regulating this matter, and this happened at a Presidency session on the 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that. We'll get to that, I promise you. Okay. If we go on to the next document, P 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, I'm looking at the deliberations and the discussions related to the adoption of these decrees, and the impression you get as an outsider is that a true democratic debate and discussion has been going on between all the present members of this assembly or meeting, and Mr. Boban is just one speaker amongst others and that the adoption of this -- these decrees on a collective basis is something that creates a commitment for everyone. Would we be wrong in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the minutes one may conclude that the decree was not challenged in any way and there were no proposals to amend it. As for this decree that we are discussing specifically right now about military district courts, there was no debate on it and it was unanimously adopted as such. The fact remains that at sessions of the Presidency there weren't any debates in terms of what one could expect in a regular parliament in the Assembly of a state or a regional community. The reasons for that were probably many-fold. One of these reasons is probably the fact that the structure of the Presidency of the HZ HB was a single-party one. I think that in the structure of the Presidency there weren't any members of any other party. I'm not sure whether that was the case, even if there were some I'm sure they were few and far between. Practically, we had a one-party Presidency. As I said, we did not have a classical opposition that would lend itself to debate, challenges, and so on, what an opposition usually does in terms of having different views. You asked me about the participants and their discussions. Yes, they did discuss different issues. Perhaps what is characteristic is what we will find on page 2, I believe, of the minutes. Mijo Tokic from Tomislavgrad takes the floor, that is page 2, paragraph 4 of the minutes. I'm saying this in relation to the question that I put a few moments ago because we will see here that Mr. Mijo Tokic, who is the head of the municipality of Tomislavgrad, says the Kupres front and Rama are fully supported by the municipality of Tomislavgrad, that is to say that they -- or rather, the Tomislavgrad municipality pays for all the defence expenses for Kupres and Rama. So what we discussed a few minutes ago is derived from this, namely, that municipalities tried to make do on their own and often they were compelled to finance even the needs of other municipalities. I think that that is clearly derived from these remarks of Mr. Mijo Tokic from Tomislavgrad, but this was a question that was raised previously and I do apologise for referring to it now because it really had to do with our previous topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next document, P 00302, P 00302, this is a decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and if we look at the end of the document we see Mostar, 18 November 1991; if we look at the top of the page of the first page we see September 1992; and of course if we look in the preamble it says that the said decision of 18 November 1991 was amended on 3 July 1992. Rather confusing, but perhaps you might be able to help us out very briefly so we can clarify this matter before I focus everyone's attention to a more important matter which would be covered in Article 7.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: This has to do with a technical matter as well. It is not being contested that the decision on the establishment of HZ HB was made on the 18th of November, 1991. At that time the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have its Official Gazette, it could not have made this public officially. This was made public, but not officially, as can be seen here. It was amended on the 3rd of July, 1992, and that is something that I have already discussed, its amendments on the 3rd of July, 1992. In Official Gazette number 1 from September 1992 it was published in its integral form, that is to say, including all the amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Now, before we go to Article 7 if there are any questions from the Bench concerning Roman numeral I, reasons, otherwise I'll -- which is the preamble in a sense or the reasons for the establishment. If there are no questions, I'll move on to Article 7. If we look at Article 7, it says here: "Extreme authority shall be vested in the following: "1. The President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ..." Then you have: "2. The Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which shall consist of representatives of the Croatian people in the municipal bodies of authority, the senior official thereof or the presidents of the municipal Croatian Defence Council." And I take it this is what you were telling us earlier that -- when you said that Mr. Boban became the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, this is what -- you were talking about this versus his other function which was president of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It is correct. I think that I have already answered this question when it was put to me by the President of the Chamber. It says here that this decision introduces for the first time the position of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a single, independent entity that had not existed up until the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- that's fine. That will help us. And just for clarification purposes, because you mentioned earlier that at one point Mr. Mate Boban was also president of the HVO, if we could go back very quickly - and I must apologise to everyone for not dealing with this earlier - if we look at 1D 00174 which was the decision on your appointment, we see Mate Boban president of the HVO and HZ HB. So at this point, at least when he's appointing you, May 15, 1992, it seems that he's wearing both hats, president of the HVO, president of the HZ HB, and I guess a third hat which would be the Presidency, not to mention the hat that he would have been wearing as the head of the HDZ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. I have already answered that question; namely, all the way up until the 14th or 15th of August Mate Boban held all of these offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We can -- we'll move along because that's been established. If we go on to the next document P 00424, and we don't need to dwell on them unless there are questions from the Bench because we covered -- we focused our attention on certain matters in the minutes of the meeting that took place on 3 July 1992. Here this document, P 00424, we see that this is the decree on transferring resources of the JNA. This is the article that was being referenced to in the minutes of the meeting; is that correct? This is the decree, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: I think I've already said that; however, it is explained here in Article 1. The first sentence of Article 1 says: "Socially owned resources ..." also in paragraph 2 where it says specifically: "Socially owned resources ..." This just clarifies the answer I have already provided, namely, that this has to do with resources that are socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the next document, P 09553 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And incidentally, Your Honours, if I'm moving too fast and you wish to ask a question, please just stop me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: P 09553. This is an order on the taking over of assets of the JNA, and we see at the bottom -- now, if we look at -- if you could please read the title in Croatian because in English it says: "Order." How would you -- could you just read the title of this legal instrument.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It says "decree" in both of the documents that I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're speaking about P 09553, that's the document that I'm on right now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And this is about taking over the assets of the JNA, and that's what you told us about earlier, the explanation that you gave us; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Again, we go on to the next document, 1D 001 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The signature, it says: "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna Presidency" and then: "President Mate Boban." So Mate Boban was the president of the Presidency and had the legislative function too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that posed to me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well -- no, no, I was looking at you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd be more than happy to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question that's put to me? I think that you have perceived the situation as it was in reality; namely, we said that from November when the HZ HB was established, Mr. Boban was president of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Also, we said that on the 8th of April, 1992, he also assumed the position of president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the speaker due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, he had a third capacity, that is to say, that of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and supreme commander of the armed forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if we go on to the next document, 1D 00161, we see that this is a decree on the confiscation of property of the occupier and transfer of ownership of the property of the occupier, and at the bottom we see president of the HVO and HZ HB Mate Boban. It's dated 3 July 1992. Again, this is one of the legal instruments that were being discussed during the minutes of the meeting that we saw; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: It is correct that that is one of the regulations that was passed then; however, perhaps it may be important to note that if certain resources were being taken over it only pertains to Article 1 (a), organization of the bodies of the former federation, that is to say, Yugoslavia. I'm not aware of a single case when property was taken over from categories (b), (c), and (d) respectively. That is to say, that I personally do not know about a single case of property being taken over from enterprises whose seats were in Serbia and Montenegro or of physical persons who were from Serbia or Montenegro or Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, P 002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask again a question about that particular document, that is 1D 00161. The -- which is important decree on the confiscation of the property of the occupier and transfer of ownership of the property of the occupier to the Croatian Community. Now, in that decree in itself I do not see the very explanation who the occupier was and what kind of property should be meant on the -- in accordance with this decree. So of course we all know that that had been the JNA attack that at that time people spoke JNA and Chetniks, et cetera. But I believe that in a legal document of this important order and the consequences of it, then probably one would expect a kind of definition about the occupier. So my question is, to you, that -- do you think that the occupier as such was already an accepted legal entity, a determination, and do you think that this -- the implementation of this decree would have caused any problem as far as the very impression which kind of property should be confiscated from the occupier or it was very clear to whom this decree was concerned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The names of the aggressors and occupiers of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been defined by the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the proclamation of a state of war on the 25th -- or rather, on the 26th in 1992. In the preamble of this decision it is stated that aggressors against Bosnia-Herzegovina are the Yugoslav People's Army; the units of the SDS, the Serb army; and I think that a reference was made there to paramilitary units arriving from the Republic of Serbia. So as a political party it's the SDS that was referred to and also the Yugoslav People's Army was referred to. Also what is noted in this decision on the declaration of a state of war is that two-thirds of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been occupied so the aggressors were named, the occupiers were named, also the fact that two-thirds of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina were already occupied. As for this decree, if you're asking me about my opinion then, just like the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it reminds one very, very much of the decisions that were made by the Partisan Liberation Movement during the Second World War. Like the people's committees during the Second World War unified all branches of government, the executive, the legislative, and the judiciary, I think that the HZ HB used this as an example to bring all three together. However, we do have to realize that the antifascist council of the national liberation of Yugoslavia made this kind of decision at its second session when property was confiscated from the occupiers and those who collaborated with the occupiers. The members of the Presidency, since they were well-versed in history, seemingly paid more attention to history than to law in both cases, like the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB in its original decision does not invoke the constitution or law on the basis of which it was adopted, although there were strong constitutional foundations for the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, this is lacking; however, there is this historical dimension, just like in this case there is the decision of the antifascist council of the national liberation of Yugoslavia, on the confiscation of the property of the aggressor and their collaborators. When I'm saying this, I'm actually referring to what I thought was a decisive factor at that point in time, namely, why this decree was passed, or rather, this decision to establish the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I thank you for the explanation. My only remaining question is as follows. If I understood well what you have explained to us, this particular decree may be related to the legal entities of the previously JNA and "Chetniks" property and it was not related to an "average" citizen of the given territory, that is, Herceg-Bosna every citizen of Serbian origin. It is my question and, frankly, that is why I ask the question if the very lack of definition wouldn't result in certain, let us be frank, injustices or actions which were directed against the ordinary citizens of the territory concerned. If it is not very clear, let me repeat. Couldn't it be possible that upon the application of this decree not only those who had been responsible for the aggression and their properties were confiscated, but also average citizens of that time Herzegovina of Serbian origin who lived at that very territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for this question. I think that I understand it and I think that I have answered it only in part. Yes, this was passed and published in the Official Gazette of the HZ HB; however, I also said that I was not aware of a single case in which property was taken away in accordance with this decree from any citizen of Serb ethnicity who was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro or Serbia. What was done was seizing the property of the Yugoslav People's Army and the federal secretariat of national defence. As a rule, it primarily consisted of barracks, that is to say, military facilities that the Yugoslav People's Army had left or the HVO took these barracks in combat with the Yugoslav People's Army. When saying this, I mean that in practice I'm not aware of a single case in which on the basis of this decree the property of any citizen was taken away by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a decree that foresees the confiscation of property can be legally justified when it relates to confiscating property belonging to an entity such as the JNA that is being dismantled, that is leaving, someone might as well occupy the barracks. But as my colleague said, let's take the case of the average Serb citizen, I don't know if this existed but let's say a hairdresser, a Serb hairdresser in Mostar, the JNA leaves for its own reasons and for his own reason he decides to leave as well. What would become of his apartment and hair salon? They could be confiscated, but was there a process of compensation and was it foreseen that they could be given back to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not defending the meaning of this decree. I'm not claiming that it's fair or reasonable. So from that point of view I think that in its paragraphs (b), (c), and (d), as I've already said, it is not justified and that it does not contain a reasonable justification for the passing of such a decree in 1 (b), (c), and (d). However, also I pointed out what the reasons were for passing such a decision. I have to point out once again that as a lawyer I cannot justify the point of (b), (c), and (d) in this decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, after the Dayton Accords, were there -- was there any litigation involving people whose property was seized? Were there trials, legal proceedings? Or were there no problems of this type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did not clarify sufficiently. When I say property owned by physical persons or natural persons, I'm referring to property in the traditional sense, as understood by us lawyers. There were violations in this respect, there was occupation of abandoned flats which were not privately owned but socially owned. After the JNA abandoned Mostar, a large number of empty military flats remained which were socially owned, but there were also flats inhabited by citizens of Serb ethnicity but these flats were socially owned. These citizens did have tenancy rights. I don't know whether I need to clarify what ownership means as opposed to tenancy rights in a socially owned flat. I also wish to mention that the legal provisions then in force governing the subject matter of socially owned flats envisioned that if a socially owned flat was abandoned and not lived in for longer than six months, tenancy rights would be forfeit because they were not equal to property rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as I'm concerned with regard to socially owned property I don't see any problem at first glance. My question relates to private property of a Serb who has his own small flat because he bought this flat or perhaps inherited it and he decides to leave, and then someone else occupies his flat. That's the problem that I'm contemplating. Was this a widespread phenomenon or was it really marginal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may have been isolated instances of that on a personal level, but I'm not aware of a single case where the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Defence Council adopted any decision whereby private property would be taken over into the ownership of the Croatian community or of the HVO. Your Honours, I'm not aware of a single such instance throughout the war period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where a lot of problems did arise was where flats were abandoned which were socially owned and tenancy rights were enjoyed by citizens of Serb ethnicity. There were quite a few problems, but the HZ HB did not take ownership of these flats unless they were military flats. Military flats were a separate category in item (a), and that did happen, taking over flats belonging -- flats used by the former JNA and so-called SSNO, and that's under item (a), Article 1, item (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at some point we will -- not with this witness but perhaps with another one, we will go over the law on the use of abandoned properties. You will see the measures that were taken which will become very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, P 00292, P 00292. Again, this is 3 July 1992. This is a decree on the treatment of persons captured in armed fighting, and of course in Article 1 we see that they are to be accorded the protections under the Geneva Convention relative to the treatment of prisoners of war. And then Article 2, it says here, and this is where I want you to comment on, it says: "The Head of the Justice and Administration Department, in cooperation with the Head of the Defence Department and the Head of the Department of Interior shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept, in accordance with the provisions of the aforementioned Convention of Article 1 of this Decree." And of course if you look at Article -- before I pose my question, if we look at Article 3 it says: "The Defence Department shall be in charge of the facilities ..." and that's a rather straightforward article, but nonetheless in Article 2 it says that you along with the other heads are to designate that location. Can you give us an explanation exactly, you know, how was this particular article to be implemented and how was it, in fact, implemented to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Correct. This is a decree adopted on the 3rd of July also at the Presidency session we've already mentioned, and what I can say -- in 1992. And what I can say about this decree is that in any war, including this one, there were prisoners of war. I don't think it's possible to wage war without having prisoners of war. I also think it was necessary to adopt a regulation governing this issue. Article 1 clearly states that the Geneva Conventions apply to persons who are captured, and Article 2 prescribes how locations will be designated where prisoners of war will be kept, whereas Article 3 specifies who is to be in charge of these facilities so that the justice and administration department in cooperation with the defence department and the department of the interior shall deal with these issues. And Article 3 provides that the defence department shall be in charge of the facilities. The decree I think is clear and I've already stated its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, to the extent that we have Article 2, can you please explain to us to what extent were you engaged in -- along with the other two department heads in trying to designate locations where prisoners would be kept, prisoners of war, pursuant to this particular decree which was signed by Mate Boban on 3 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC
utterances.text: Well, this needs a brief clarification. On the entire territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the 30 municipalities mentioned in the decree on the establishment of the HZ HB, there was not a single facility used for people serving prison sentences. The only thing we had at that time was the district investigative or a remand prison in Mostar. It was attached to the higher court in Mostar. It was not an establishment where sentences could be served, but a remand prison for persons under investigation. Immediately after taking up my duty as head of the department of justice and general administration, I talked to the governor of this establishment in Mostar and he informed me of the situation in the district prison in Mostar, where apart from persons serving prison sentences there was also a certain number of prisoners of war who were in the prison without any court decision having been issued. And of course this had to be dealt with. Soon after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to stop you right there because we have a procedural motion to discuss. The Prosecution -- but it's an important question so I think we will come back to it tomorrow, Mr. Karnavas will come back to this question tomorrow. So, Witness, I will ask the usher to escort you out of the room and I would ask you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00 for our hearing that will take place in the morning. So I'm not sure who would like to take the floor first, the Prosecution or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, this is, for counsel and everyone else, it's unrelated to this witness. It relates to a witness from last week, Professor Jankovic. And we'd been asked to make sure that the record reflects that the -- the submission that was filed last Friday by the Prosecution which was our objections to the documents tendered by the Praljak Defence to the exhibits they were tendering through Professor Jankovic, we filed a document, a written filing, objecting to those and it had some documents attached to an annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it was filed normally, as the Trial Chamber knows, these are handled strictly by the IC document procedure that's been in place, but this one we thought was a little bit unusual because we had a couple of arguments to make and some documents to attach to it. So we made it into a real filing which we filed on Friday. We made that filing before the registrar had officially assigned an IC number to the submission of exhibits by the Praljak Defence. And so for the record the filing of the Prosecution from last Friday objecting to the Jankovic -- or some -- to some of the Jankovic exhibits, not all of them, is, in fact, applying to the Defence exhibits which are tendered via IC number 823-3D. So apparently it created a little bit of procedural confusion. We made the filing early so that counsel could read it over the weekend and make a response if he wanted to. The time-frame on the submissions and the responses on tendering exhibits is rather short, and so we went ahead and filed the document even though it had not yet been officially tendered by the Praljak Defence. So again just to clarify, the Prosecution filing on the Jankovic exhibits that was made last Friday applies to the IC number 823-3D exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague has explained what this is about. We feel it needs to be placed clearly on record. As my colleague said, on the 3rd of July, the Defence of General Praljak submitted the usual IC list, expecting it to be received today and to be allocated a number, as we've been doing for the past two years; but for the reasons he stated which I fully take into account, the Prosecutor responded on the 4th of July, the very next day, before the IC list became a formal document because it hadn't yet been given a number. So I carefully re-read your decision of the 4th of April simply to be on the safe side, as that decision in paragraph 32 mentions dead-lines and other interpretations are possible, so to be on the safe side I felt it was better for me to respond within 24 hours which I did. And this filing was also received as was the filing mentioned by my learned friend. Both filings, I think I can say, have to do with the IC number 823 given today, so that is the position of the Prosecutor and the response to your decision guide-line 8. We both understand that we should not respond to such submissions until the IC list is given a number. That's the crux of the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for clarifying this issue, both the Prosecution and the Defence. So we understand that the problem relates to -- or the filing, rather, relates to IC number 823. It is now 7.00. Mr. Karnavas, you have used up almost two hours, 1 hour, 59 minutes and a few seconds but I'll let you have those seconds, but almost two hours. We meet tomorrow morning at 9.00. Have a very good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
